items.summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
items.title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

items.summary: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
items.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models

items.summary: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
items.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models

items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: Online search activity is widely used as a digital trace of information seeking during epidemics, but its predictive value is often reduced to correlation, a selected lag, or a single forecast-error score. We examine eight pre-specified Google Trends-COVID-19 pairs in both directions using matched LightGBM forecasts over rolling 400-day windows and horizons of 1-14 days. Log-RMSE gain is combined with forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE), which captures horizon-dependent changes in the signed error distribution. The resulting directional predictive signature comprises response class, RMSE effect, FEDE endpoint and early-slope responses, persistence across rolling regimes, and horizon profile. For screening candidate directions, we also introduce a relative persistence-weighted directional predictive response strength (DPRS) on a within-study 0-100 scale; 100 denotes the strongest observed response in the comparison set, not an absolute coupling maximum. The pairs show concordant, RMSE-only, FEDE-only, and mixed responses. "loss of smell" -> reported cases is accuracy-dominant, with mean log-RMSE gain 0.104 (about 9.9% equivalent RMSE reduction) and DPRS 100, whereas the reverse direction is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.048; DPRS=42). "covid test" -> positive rate is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.039; positive in 72% of windows; DPRS=98) despite negative RMSE gain, while "lockdown" -> stringency is the clearest concordant case (DPRS=78). World-level symptom/case pairs are less persistent. Thus, forecast accuracy and error-distribution dynamics are complementary, predictive effects can be direction- and metric-dependent, and forecast horizon is part of the relationship. Aggregated regime-level patterns should not be extrapolated to individual time points or interpreted as evidence of causality.
items.title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Predictive Dynamics in Google Search and COVID-19 Time Series: A Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Analysis

items.summary: Reliable microstructural parameter estimation in diffusion MRI (dMRI) critically depends on the acquisition protocol. Yet, common protocol design criteria may not fully reflect estimator bias, parameter constraints, and nonlinear fitting behavior in complex inverse problems. Here, we introduce Protocol Optimization via Loss Assessing Parameter Recovery (POLAR), an end-to-end framework that searches the continuous acquisition space and directly minimizes multiparameter recovery error through noisy signal simulation and the chosen model fitting. We demonstrate POLAR spanning distinct microstructural environments: the Cylinder-Zeppelin model for white matter, Neurite Exchange Imaging (NEXI) for gray matter, and Cellular Exchange Imaging (CEXI) for permeable cells. Across independent held-out parameter sets, POLAR consistently outperformed model-specific reference designs, reducing RMSE by up to $50\%$ for Cylinder-Zeppelin and $74\%$ for CEXI, while reducing NEXI exchange time bias by $70\%$. These gains across distinct biophysical models, acquisition settings, and reference design strategies demonstrate the benefit of optimizing acquisition protocols through the downstream parameter-estimation problem. POLAR provides a flexible, model-specific and estimator-aware framework for designing dMRI protocols tailored to the microstructural parameters and experimental conditions of interest.
items.title: Diffusion MRI protocol design for reliable parameter recovery: a unified framework across biophysical models

items.summary: In the present paper, we proceed with the research initiated in (S. Antontsev \emph{et al.}, Inverse Problems, 2021). We study the inverse problem for the Kelvin--Voigt equations with $p$-Laplacian and with a right-hand side in the integral over-determination condition, which approximates a discontinuous function at $t=0$. We rescale the problem in a neighbourhood $[0,1/n]$ and pass to the limit as $n$ approaches infinity. This leads to the inverse problem on an infinitesimal initial layer, which transforms the initial velocity into a new one.
items.title: Kurzweil's impulsive inverse problem for the Kelvin--Voigt equations with $p$-Laplacian

items.summary: Unrefereed, AI-assisted research preprint. The release resolves fixed-dimensional and growing-dimensional continuation questions for deterministic network SIS trajectories, gives an explicit dimension-free Holder replacement, and derives a deterministic sampled-observation corollary. The exact supplementary checks do not machine-verify the universal analytic proofs.
items.title: Reconstruction and continuation in network SIS epidemics

items.summary: In this work, we study a fractional diffusion model in time and space, formulated in an open and bounded domain, involving a Caputo fractional derivative of order $μ\in(0,1)$ with respect to a time scale function $Ψ$, together with a spectral fractional Laplacian operator of order $s\in(0,1)$. The associated direct problem is analyzed, as well as the inverse problem of temporal reconstruction from final data, which is inherently ill-posed. Through a spectral representation, the instability of the problem and the effect of the choice of the function $Ψ$ on the amplification of spectral modes are examined.
items.title: Backward Homogeneous Heat Equation with $Ψ$-Caputo Time Derivative and Spectral Fractional Laplacian

items.summary: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.
items.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems

items.summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
items.title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

items.summary: This dataset contains the analysis companion for the manuscript "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia": analysis programs, derived result tables, archived validation records, and publication-rendering code. The ZIP contains 144 files and preserves the directory structure needed to distinguish repeated basenames. The study examines daily port activity in a 72-port Asian panel and reports results for 38 isolated cyclone-exposure episodes from 19 storms in 2021–2025. This archive preserves the existing analysis and diagnostic records; no statistical model was re-estimated for the journal-transfer package. Earlier project-stage labels inside the files document provenance. Provider-owned raw snapshots are not redistributed. Original analysis programs require the source inputs and paths documented in the README and source code. Historical acquisition programs have not been rerun for this deposit and may depend on earlier snapshots or live provider services; the archive is not a self-contained, one-click reconstruction of the frozen source database. Source data and documentation include IMF PortWatch, JMA best tracks, NCAR archived tropical-cyclone guidance, NOAA IBTrACS, and the World Bank Development Data Lab maritime-connections documentation. Upstream use and redistribution remain subject to the respective providers’ terms. Qi Cao, Yuhang Li, Yi’an Liang, Mengyuan Jia, and Ziran Zhou contributed equally to the associated manuscript. Its corresponding authors are Ziran Zhou and Kwi-sik Min. Author order follows the manuscript. Archive SHA-256: 1f193d4c81d4f0ba352da2ccb9174f00e1eb4eb153f4f2e0fcd4c4744bb7c12f.
items.title: Analysis code and derived results for "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia"

items.summary: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.
items.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization

items.summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
items.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents

items.summary: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.
items.title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control

items.summary: Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and claim denials, yet identifying the recurring, correctable patterns behind them remains largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. We present Pattern Intelligence, a deployed system that discovers such patterns without supervision by clustering claims on their adjudication behaviour rather than their identity. Each claim is embedded in a 130-dimensional vector combining per-line expected-versus-actual payment ratios, claim adjustment reason (CARC) codes, denial and payment signals, and service composition. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric - we show they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups - and are reintroduced only as a post-hoc segmentation (by contract and visit type) that keeps every surfaced pattern coherent and actionable. We cluster with HDBSCAN, recover structure from the noise set via second-pass sub-clustering, and gate low-confidence memberships. A large language model translates each centroid into an analyst-ready description of dominant procedures, adjustment reasons, and failure mode. We report a recurring finding: roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials, depending on tenant and segmentation, form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration or representation we tried groups - a domain property, we argue, rather than a modeling deficiency. We evaluate validity through cluster-coherence analysis and quantify impact with a recoverable-opportunity ($) metric on two production tenants (approx. 10K and 157K claims) within a six-tenant deployment. Rather than a new algorithm, the contribution is a problem formulation, a representation-design insight, and empirical findings from production.
items.title: Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised, LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Systematic Underpayment and Denial Patterns in Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management

The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
items.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models

items.summary: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.
items.title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control

items.summary: Safe autonomous navigation of UASs requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid system, or runtime assurance mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
items.title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides

items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
items.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction

items.summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; ac
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

items.summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-cont
items.title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

items.summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

items.summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoher
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

items.summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmar
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

items.summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.
tags: spiking neural networks; edge pest detection; thermal sensing; energy-accuracy trade-off; computer a
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Spiking Neural Networks for Computer Agriculture Edge Pest-Detection Under Thermal-Sensor Power Constraints: An Artificial Intelligence Energy-Accuracy Trade-off Audit for Field-Deployment Safety
